item.title: HoneyLabs Intelligence - v1.2.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
1.2.0 is built for the triage queue rather than the demo. New feed input, fingerprints: TLS (JA4) and HTTP request (Akin) fingerprints the HoneyLabs sensors saw from 20 or more addresses in the shape of a scanning tool, with population counts and the port and path they favour. A scheduled search keeps it in the honeylabs\_fingerprints lookup, so a lookup on the JA4 field of your own TLS logs (Zeek ssl.log carries one) flags a scanning client on your perimeter with no API call, even when the address is clean. The Triage dashboard gains a fourth panel on it. Without a key the feed carries the 500 most widespread shapes of the last 7 days; with a free key stored on the setup page the input pulls the full list over 30 days. The honeylabs enrichment command returns honeylabs\_cves: the CVEs whose exploit paths the address probed in the last 7 days, so an alert can say what the address was after and a correlation search can join it against what you are exposed to. honeylabssearch mode\=similar takes an Akin token from your own web, WAF or proxy logs and returns the request shapes within a few headers of it, what those clients ask for, and the family it belongs to. Three alerts ship switched off, each with a 24 hour throttle per indicator: inbound from active exploiters, outbound to captured malware infrastructure, and a coordinated scanner client on the perimeter. Every row carries an evidence link. HTTP request fingerprints are Akin tokens (https://github.com/honeylabshq/akin). fp\_type\=akin works in mode\=fingerprint and mode\=population, and mode\=events takes an akin\= filter. fp\_type\=ja4h reports that the type was retired instead of failing the search.


Short Description:
Threat intelligence from live honeypot sensors, in SPL. Enrich any IP field with a verdict, ASN, ports and first and last seen, or query the dataset directly: raw probes, request payloads, CVE exploitation, JA4 fingerprints, top attackers. Plus two hourly threat feeds. Free API key gives 500 lookups a day; no key gives 10.


Description:
HoneyLabs runs open-source honeypot sensors on the public internet. Nothing reaches them by accident, so every connection they record is a scan, a probe, a brute-force attempt or an exploit. There are no false positives to filter out, because there is no legitimate traffic to confuse them with. This app puts that dataset inside Splunk. Two search commands. The first enriches addresses you already have. Point it at any field holding a public IPv4 address and it annotates every event: index=firewall | honeylabs field=src_ip | where honeylabs_events > 0 It writes back verdict, verdict_key, network_type, events, first_seen, last_seen, country, asn, asn_org, rdns, top_port, ports, exploit_hits and reference, each prefixed honeylabs_ so nothing collides with your own fields. Addresses are de-duplicated per search, so an index carrying the same scanner across ten thousand events costs one lookup. The second queries the honeypot dataset directly, with no local data required. Nine modes cover raw events, captured request payloads, top attackers, timelines, ASN profiles, TLS and HTTP fingerprints, IOC and CIDR lookups, CVE exploitation, and fingerprint population counts. Use it to answer questions your own logs cannot: who else is exercising this CVE, what payload is being sent, which other sources share this JA4 fingerprint. Two modular inputs, shipped disabled, index active exploiter addresses and captured malware staging URLs on an hourly schedule. Neither needs credentials. Two dashboards ship with the app: an overview of what the feeds currently carry, and an explorer for querying the dataset without writing SPL by hand. About the API key. The app installs and runs with no account and no setup, but anonymous use is capped at 10 lookups a day, which is enough to try the commands and not enough to work with. A free key raises that to 500 a day and takes about a minute to create at https://honeylabs.net/dashboard. Paste it into the app's setup page; it is stored through Splunk's storage/passwords, encrypted at rest, and never written to a .conf file. Paid plans go to 50,000 a day. On privacy: a lookup sends only the public IP addresses in your search. Not your index, host, source or sourcetype names, not your Splunk version, not the search string. Private, loopback, link-local, multicast and reserved addresses are filtered out locally before the request is built. The feed inputs are ordinary HTTPS downloads of a public file and disclose nothing at all. Running Enterprise Security? Load the indicator feeds through its own threat intelligence framework so they reach correlation searches and risk scoring rather than only being searchable, and keep these commands for on-demand investigation. Walkthrough: https://honeylabs.net/integrations/splunk-es

item.title: TA-Vulnerability catalog - v1.1.0 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**# TA-Vulnerability catalog 1.1.0 — Release notes** Released: 2026-09-19 Previous version: 1.0.0 **---** **## New features** **\*\*CISA Vulnrichment data input\*\*** A third data source has been added: the CISA Vulnrichment repository (\`cisagov/vulnrichment\`), indexed under the new sourcetype \`vulninfo:vulnrichment\`. \* The first run streams the branch tarball and indexes every record, without consuming the   GitHub API rate limit. Subsequent runs walk the GitHub Commits API from the last processed   commit SHA and index only the CVE files that were added or changed. \* Events retain the **\*\*complete raw CVE Record 5.x JSON\*\***, with CIM fields extracted in front   of it — nothing from the source record is discarded. \* CISA ADP enrichment is exposed as searchable fields: SSVC decision points   (\`ssvc\_exploitation\`, \`ssvc\_automatable\`, \`ssvc\_technical\_impact\`), KEV membership   (\`is\_known\_exploited\`, \`kev\_date\_added\`), CVSS vectors and CWE identifiers. \* Mapped to the CIM **\*\*Vulnerabilities\*\*** data model: \`cve\`, \`signature\`, \`cvss\`, \`severity\`,   \`severity\_id\`, \`cwe\`, \`category\`, \`vendor\_product\`, \`url\`, \`xref\`, \`vuln\_published\_time\`,   \`vuln\_modified\_time\`, \`dest\`, \`dvc\`. \* A GitHub personal access token can optionally be configured to raise the API rate limit   from 60 to 5,000 requests per hour. No token scopes are required. \* \`Seed max files\` allows the initial full load to be split across several runs, resuming   from the same pinned commit snapshot. **\*\*Full reload option on every input\*\*** All three inputs now have a \`Full reload\` checkbox. When enabled, the input ignores its checkpoint and re-ingests the entire dataset on the next run — useful after changing the destination index or losing indexed data. A warning is logged on every run while it is on, as a reminder to turn it back off. **\*\*Expanded CIM coverage for the KEV catalog\*\*** \`vulninfo:kevcatalog\` now populates \`dest\`, \`dvc\` and \`severity\_id\`, which were previously absent. KEV rows in the Vulnerabilities data model are no longer missing \`dest\`. **---** **## Fixes** **\*\*Checkpoints are now scoped per input instance\*\*** The KEV and EPSS inputs previously stored their progress under a fixed checkpoint key, shared by every instance of that input. As a result, running two instances of the same input caused them to overwrite each other's progress, and deleting and recreating an input under a different name did not start from a clean state. Checkpoint keys now include the input instance name (\`kev\_catalog\_state\_v2\_\\`, \`epss\_last\_score\_date\_\\`), so instances are fully independent. **\*\*Upgrading does not cause re-ingestion:\*\*** on the first run after upgrade, each input adopts the value from its old key and logs the migration. **\*\*EPSS no longer risks repeated full re-ingestion\*\*** The EPSS input used the snapshot's \`score\_date\` — read from the CSV header comment — as its checkpoint, and skipped saving the checkpoint entirely when that value could not be parsed. If the upstream header format ever changed, the checkpoint would never advance and the full snapshot (300,000+ events) would be re-indexed on every interval, duplicating indefinitely. The checkpoint is now always saved. When \`score\_date\` is unavailable, a hash of the snapshot content is used instead, and a warning is logged. Collection continues normally and unchanged snapshots are still skipped. **\*\*EPSS events removed from the CIM Vulnerabilities data model\*\*** \`vulninfo:epss\` carried a custom \`epss\` tag that matched no data model, which produced a warning in the add-on's data model mapping and placed the events in no dataset. EPSS scores are per-CVE probabilities rather than vulnerability records, so the mapping has been removed rather than completed. EPSS events remain fully searchable and are intended to be joined to the other sourcetypes on \`cve\`. **---** **## Upgrade notes** \* **\*\*Restart Splunk after upgrading.\*\*** The add-on adds a new modular input and new input   parameters; splunkd must re-read \`inputs.conf.spec\` before they take effect. \* **\*\*No re-ingestion occurs for existing inputs.\*\*** Legacy checkpoints migrate automatically on   the first run. The migration is logged:   \`index\=\_internal source\=\*ta\_vulnerability\_catalog\* "checkpoint migrated"\` \* **\*\*Before enabling the Vulnrichment input, check your license headroom.\*\*** The initial load   is 130,000–200,000 events at several KB to tens of KB each. \* **\*\*If you built searches on \`tag\=epss\`\*\***, switch them to \`sourcetype\=vulninfo:epss\`. The   eventtype and tag no longer exist. \* Each input must be enabled on exactly one node. Checkpoints are stored per node, so running   the same input on several nodes produces duplicate events. \------------------------------8\< note in Japanese------------------------------ **# リポジトリ（\`cisagov/vulnrichment\`）の取り込みに対応しました。新しい sourcetype \`vulninfo:vulnrichment\` でインデックスされます。 \* 初回はブランチの tarball をストリーミング展開して全件を取り込みます。GitHub API のレート制限を消費しません。2回目以降は、最後に処理したコミット SHA を起点にGitHub Description:

The app includes built-in controls to limit data exposure, including a mandatory capability requirement, configurable row limits, audit logging to the internal index, and cache management through KV store. Administrators must configure a TypeSafe API key before the command becomes operational. All API communication occurs over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai by default. The MISP Splunk Add-on is a specialized integration tool that seamlessly ingests threat intelligence data from the Malware Information Sharing Platform (MISP) into Splunk. The add-on enables organisations to centralize and analyze Indicators of Compromise (IOCs), threat events, attributes, and other intelligence shared via MISP, providing security teams with enhanced visibility into evolving cyber threats. A key strength of the add-on is its ability to normalize MISP data into structured Splunk events, making threat indicators such as IP addresses, domains, URLs, file hashes, email addresses, malware samples, and event metadata easily searchable and available for correlation with existing security logs. This enables faster threat detection, investigation, and incident response. The add-on supports flexible configuration options, including customizable polling intervals, incremental data collection through checkpointing, secure API key authentication, SSL verification, and enterprise proxy support for deployments operating behind corporate firewalls. These capabilities make the add-on suitable for a wide range of enterprise environments. Compatible with Splunk Enterprise 10.0.0 and later, the MISP Splunk Add-on stores all collected threat intelligence in configurable Splunk indexes, allowing analysts to leverage Splunk's powerful search, dashboards, alerts, and correlation capabilities. item.title: Supply Chain and AI Threat Intelligence Platform - v1.2.17 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:

SCIP v1.2.17 — MITRE ATLAS coverage expansion, severity re-rating, compliance citation corrections, and audit fixes

This release consolidates the work in v1.2.15, v1.2.16 and v1.2.17 since the last published release (v1.2.14). The AI/agentic detection library grows from 66 to 81 rules (72 MITRE ATLAS-mapped, 9 vendor-defined). No cryptographic surface was modified.

New detections (15)

Fifteen new AI and agentic threat detections were added, covering: an AI service API used as a covert command-and-control channel; AI supply-chain rug pulls, where an established component's newly published content turns malicious; artifact repositories used as dead-drop C2 channels; agent runtime capability discovery; and sub-technique coverage for dataset and capability acquisition, autonomous exploit and agent tool development, system prompt and instruction discovery, agent tool data collection, tool runtime response poisoning, and poisoned model, dataset and agent-tool publication.

Separately, two existing detections gain additional technique tags, for multimodal prompt-injection triggers and for misconfigured or publicly exposed AI services. These are more precise labels on rules that already shipped, not new detections.

Detection accuracy and severity

  • Every ATLAS rule and the SBOM Drift Monitor now set alert.severity as an integer. String values were being coerced by Splunk and read back as 0, so triggered-alert severity in Splunk and any alert action keyed on it were unusable. Emitted severity fields, lookups and dashboard behaviour are unchanged.
  • A severity rubric pass re-rated three rules added in the previous release and confirmed nine others.
  • Five MITRE ATLAS technique names and tactics were corrected to the catalog text, and coverage is now scoped against ATLAS 2026.09 with a recorded disposition for every technique added in that catalog release.
  • Three regression guards now run before every package build: one validates every technique stamp against the shipped lookup, including secondary stamps; one validates the severity mapping on every rule; and one verifies that shared facts agree across the README, the deployment guide and the shipped artifacts.

Compliance citation corrections

No assessment logic changed. Citations and control identifiers were corrected across seven of the nine frameworks SCIP assesses:

  • EU Cyber Resilience Act control IDs now use the regulation's own Annex and Article labels; two transposed points corrected; coverage added for two security-update provisions. Now 21 controls.
  • FDA 524B: transposed statutory citations corrected, the patch-cycle control re-cited, the cyber device definition restored to its three statutory prongs, and guidance-derived rows distinguished from statutory ones. Now 21 controls.
  • NIST CSF 2.0: 16 subcategory descriptions replaced with CSF 2.0 outcome text.
  • PCI DSS 4.0.1 and FedRAMP: requirement and control titles restored to official text.
  • HIPAA: four rows re-titled to the standard's own name; a control that was being assessed twice is now out of scope.
  • DORA: incident classification and ICT concentration risk re-cited.
  • A nightly cleanup now retires status records for controls that are no longer in scope, so renamed or descoped controls leave nothing frozen behind.
  • Compliance views and the CSV export now carry a Last Assessed column, flagging any status older than two days as stale.

Functional fixes

  • The POA&M population search collided its inline time bounds with its dispatch window and scanned nothing while reporting success.
  • Five scheduled searches stored a search string beginning with a literal search command, which silently excluded events whose raw text lacked that word.
  • Setup, Remediation Tracking and Telemetry Settings could write to the KV Store on page load, before any Save action. All three now write only on an explicit action.
  • Telemetry Settings rewrote the license collection on every page view; it now updates a single record on an explicit selection.
  • The license status check treated a record with a missing or non-numeric expiry as active.
  • Risk score pruning deleted rows with a missing or non-numeric timestamp; those rows are now retained.
  • Incomplete SBOM baseline rows no longer suppress the set-a-baseline prompts or count toward baselined-application totals.

Setup and onboarding

  • The Setup page now names every index SCIP requires, states that SCIP does not create them, gives both standalone and clustered paths, and warns when any is missing.
  • A new section explains that SBOM drift's component, version and count signals are inactive until a baseline is set.
  • The file monitor section states that both SBOM inputs ship disabled, that the monitored path must be repointed, and that SPDX files belong in their own directory.
  • NVD API key copy corrected in four places.
  • The license blocklist field no longer shows an internal placeholder on load, and the blocklist is emptied through an explicit Clear action.

Air-gapped and egress-restricted deployments

CISA KEV and EPSS threat intelligence can now be refreshed by file transfer, as NVD and OSV already could. Both feeds write normalized records to spool directories that new file-monitor inputs index. Previously both were script-only, so without outbound access they stayed frozen at install, silently degrading KEV-driven risk scoring. The IL Deployment Guide documents the record formats and procedure.

Roles and user experience

All three SCIP roles gain eleven read and UI capabilities that restore the Apps menu icons and the Setup credential-status read. The administrative role retains the capabilities its credential-save controls require.

Documentation

New ATLAS coverage manifest and a guide to authoring your own ATLAS detections on top of the shipped baseline. The deployment guide now lists every required index in both its standalone and clustered instructions, documents scheduled searches that ship disabled by design, and corrects the outbound-connection table, which described telemetry as opt-out. Telemetry is opt-in and off by default.

Upgrade notes

  • Role assignment. SCIP roles are additive. If a user was assigned a SCIP role as their only role, they have been without the top-right username and account menu since v1.1.11. Assign your organization's base Splunk role alongside the SCIP role.
  • Saved-search renames. EU CRA and FDA compliance saved searches were renamed to match their new control identifiers. Any local override or external reference to the old stanza names must be updated.
  • Alert severity. Triggered-alert severity now reports real values instead of 0. Alert actions keyed on severity will begin seeing 2 through 5.
  • HIPAA control count drops from 9 to 8 in-scope controls. The descoped control's saved search is disabled rather than deleted, preserving the audit trail.

item.description:

Release Notes:
* CRITICAL: disconnect\_cause was declared twice in the Stop record field list, at positions 17 and 134. Splunk took the first, so for three releases the field held Oracle's coarse outcome category and the Q.850 cause at position 134 had no field name at all and could not be searched. Position 17 is now cisco\_disconnect\_cause, which is Oracle's own name for it, and disconnect\_cause now holds the Q.850 cause. If you have saved searches or dashboards matching on disconnect\_cause values, they are matching the coarse category and need to move to cisco\_disconnect\_cause. * CRITICAL: calling\_mos, called\_mos, calling\_r\_factor and called\_r\_factor now hold the actual score. Oracle writes all four multiplied by 100 so that an integer attribute can carry a fraction - a MOS of 4.3 arrives on the wire as 430 - and the fields previously passed that through, so any threshold written against them was wrong by two orders of magnitude. The wire value is still available as calling\_mos\_raw and so on. A zero in these columns means the SBC has no QoS feature set enabled rather than a call scoring 0.0, so zero now reads as null. * The app now extracts a ciscoguid from accounting\_call\_id, so SBC records can be rolled up with CUCM, CUBE and CVP data where the deployment carries the identifier across. * Added worst\_mos and worst\_r\_factor, the score of the worse of the two directions. For some statistical analysis end-users will want to exclude the "not bad" side. These new fields will now let them do that more easily. * Oracle SBC CDR's two disconnect cause spaces are finally extracted as separate fields. Added q850\_cause\_description and cisco\_cause\_description, which describe the two cause spaces separately, from a new cause\_descriptions lookup. * the now-general "cause\_description" values now list the most specific reason available: the Q.850 cause where there is a meaningful one, and Oracle's coarse category where there is not. Prior to this release, cause\_description was simply giving the RADIUS accounting termination cause (still available as accounting\_termination\_cause\_description). * Added a ciscoguid\_family field, which reports whether a ciscoguid is an H.225-format guid or a time-based UUID. This was previously only available via a search macro that misreported any record carrying two guids. * The descriptions shown for SIP response codes, ie the sip\_status\_description field, have been rewritten from the IETF specifications that define each code - RFC 3261, plus the fifteen later RFCs that define the codes RFC 3261 does not cover. The codes themselves and their reason phrases (sip\_status\_code and sip\_status\_name) are unchanged. If you have saved searches, alerts or dashboards that match on the old description text rather than on sip\_status\_code, update them. * Added a health check that lists any saved search, dashboard or macro still using the old west/east media flow field names, with the name that replaces each. Run it as a user with admin\_all\_objects for a complete inventory. * Added a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md file to the app, itemizing the third-party components it bundles and the origin of the data in each of its reference lookups.

item.title: Add-on for Prisma Cloud Audit - v2.0.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
### Fixed * **Infinite loop / stuck input process.** Every failure path (auth call fails, no token in auth response, data call fails, empty result page) previously logged an error and looped back immediately with no exit condition — the modular input would spin forever, re-hitting the Prisma Cloud API with no backoff, and never exit. All paths now terminate the run. * **Unhandled crash on non-JSON error bodies (`JSONDecodeError`).** `response.json()` / `auth_response.json()` were called inline inside `.format()` calls with no error handling. A 5xx response with an empty or non-JSON body raised an uncaught `JSONDecodeError`, killing the script with a raw traceback instead of a clean log line. Both the auth response and the data response JSON parsing are now wrapped in `try/except ValueError`, logging the raw response text and exiting cleanly. * **Silent error messages.** `"error in data collection".format(response.json())` and similar calls had no `{}` placeholder, so the parsed response body was discarded — errors logged with zero detail. Now logs the actual response body (`response.text` / `auth_response.text`). * **Misleading exit-condition log message.** The message logged when there's nothing new to collect said `"end_date>start_date.existing the script!"`, which was backwards (it fires when `start_date >= end_date`) and had a typo. Corrected to `"start_date>=end_date, nothing new to collect. exiting the script!"`. * **Empty-page handling.** A data response with no `value` records previously skipped the entire pagination/checkpoint block, leaving `keep_running` untouched — another path into the infinite loop. Now logs, saves a checkpoint, and exits cleanly. ### Changed * Genuine failures (auth failure, missing token, data-fetch HTTP error, malformed JSON, checkpoint-save exception) now `raise RuntimeError(...)` instead of just logging. This surfaces failed runs to the `splunktaucclib` framework (which logs the traceback and marks the run as failed) instead of exiting silently as if successful — important for noticing things like bad credentials or persistent API errors. * Benign "nothing to do" cases (no new time range, no records this cycle) still exit cleanly without raising, since they aren't errors. ### Removed * Dead code: an unused `headers` dict (apikey-style auth header) that was built but never passed to any request — the actual calls use `auth_headers` / `data_headers`. ### Verified * `python3 -m py_compile` passes with no syntax errors. * Confirmed against a live 500-error and JSON-decode-error traceback, and a live invalid-credentials scenario — both now produce a single clean `RuntimeError` with the real API error message instead of a raw crash or silent infinite retry. ###

Instead of re-sending your entire vulnerability snapshot on every poll, it tracks each vulnerability's lifecycle and sends only what changed: opened, updated, or fixed. Benefits: * Dramatically fewer and smaller events, since unchanged findings are no longer re-sent every cycle. * Accurate event timestamps reflecting when a vulnerability was actually detected or fixed, not just when the input happened to run. * Correctly groups vulnerabilities across all workload types, including Kubernetes, AWS Lambda, ECS, Cloud Run, Azure Container services, and containers running directly on hosts, so a workload's vulnerability history stays stable and doesn't flip between fixed and reopened without a real change. Note that workloads running multiple containers may report a few more findings than a single combined one would, since each container is tracked individually for an accurate "currently in use" status. * Faster, simpler searches: | tstats latest(state) by finding\_id | where state!\="fixed" * gives you current posture directly, instead of aggregating a full daily dump. The existing input keeps working exactly as before under its own sourcetype, so upgrading is non-breaking. You can run both side by side, or switch your dashboards to the new sourcetype (sysdig:secure:vulnerability\_findings) at your own pace. See the add-on's documentation for setup and example searches. **Fixed: Splunk Cloud compatibility** The add-on has been rebuilt on the current Splunk UCC framework, resolving a Splunk Cloud Platform compatibility issue flagged by Splunk on the previous release. **Compatibility** Supports Python 3.9 and 3.13 (Splunk Enterprise 9.4–10.5).

Description:
The Cisco Security Cloud application offers seamless integration for connecting your Cisco devices with Splunk. It features a modular UX input design, built-in health checks, and constant monitoring to ensure operational integrity. Product(s) Enabled: Cisco AI Defense Cisco Duo Cisco Email Threat Defense (ETD) Cisco Endpoint Visibility Module (EVM) CIM Mappings (Beta) Cisco Identity Intelligence (CII) Cisco Multicloud Defense Cisco NVM Cisco Secure Endpoint Cisco Secure Firewall (FTD/eStreamer/ASA) Cisco Secure Workload Cisco Isovalent Cisco Isovalent Edge Processor **Alpha Cisco Secure Malware Analytics (SMA) Cisco Secure Network Analytics (SNA) Cisco Vulnerability Intelligence Cisco XDR (Incident Import & Promote to ES Notable) Here’s the revised version with the sourcetype list and stronger 3.x transition language. **MAJOR VERSION CHANGE: CiscoSecurityCloud 4.0.0 Release Notes** CiscoSecurityCloud 4.0.0 introduces expanded Cisco Secure Firewall / FTD syslog and Advanced Logging support, with improved parsing, event routing, CIM/data model alignment, dashboard visibility, and ingestion reliability. This release adds a new FTD sourcetype routing model that separates FTD events by event family instead of keeping all events under a single generic `cisco:ftd:syslog` sourcetype. This improves field extraction accuracy, dashboard filtering, data model mapping, and long-term supportability for FTD syslog and Advanced Logging data. Because this changes how FTD events are categorized, **4.0.0 may be a breaking change for customers with custom Splunk content**. Content that may require review includes: - Saved searches, alerts, reports, and dashboards that filter only on `sourcetype="cisco:ftd:syslog"` - Custom macros, eventtypes, tags, and CIM/data model constraints - Custom props/transforms or routing assumptions for FTD syslog - Data model acceleration searches scoped to the previous FTD sourcetype - External integrations or correlation searches that expect all FTD events in one sourcetype Customers should update broad FTD searches from "cisco:ftd:syslog" to cisco:ftd:intrusion cisco:ftd:connection cisco:ftd:connection:security cisco:ftd:file cisco:ftd:malware cisco:ftd:discovery cisco:ftd:useractivity cisco:ftd:correlation cisco:ftd:intrusionpacket cisco:ftd:adv:http cisco:ftd:adv:ftp cisco:ftd:adv:conn cisco:ftd:adv:dns cisco:ftd:adv:weird cisco:ftd:adv:notice CiscoSecurityCloud 4.0.0 is intended for customers who want the new FTD Advanced Logging model and are ready to validate custom content against the expanded sourcetypes. To ease the transition, the CiscoSecurityCloud 3.x branch will be actively maintained and should remain the recommended stable branch for customers who require the existing FTD sourcetype behavior. Customers can continue using 3.x while they assess 4.0.0, update custom SPL, and validate dashboards, alerts, and data model acceleration.

The app visualizes authentication events, privileged credential access, device access patterns, and security alerts generated by Xage's Zero Trust platform. Description:
The Xage Fabric TA is a technical add-on that ingests and normalizes Xage Fabric syslog audit logs into Splunk's Common Information Model. The add-on parses RFC5424-formatted syslog messages containing JSON audit payloads, extracting authentication events, configuration changes, and security alerts. Events are automatically tagged and mapped to the CIM Authentication, Change, and Alerts data models. The add-on handles both TCP and UDP syslog inputs as well as file-based monitoring, and performs sourcetype classification at index time to ensure proper field extraction. It is designed to operate in conjunction with the companion stg_Xage app, which provides visualization dashboards and Enterprise Security correlation searches. The add-on provides field extractions, event type definitions, and CIM tags but does not include user-facing dashboards or saved searches.
